The 2022 directive (FAA AD 2022-03-07) partially supersedes the 2020 directive (FAA AD 2020-05-11) and is itself superseded by the 2024 directive (FAA AD 2024-01-02). As a result, the requirements of the 2020 and 2022 ADs are no longer in effect. Current operators must comply with the 2024 AD, which mandates MCAS Software v2.0 installation, revised FCOM procedures, and enhanced angle-of-attack monitoring. Compliance with the earlier ADs is not required for continued operation.

The regulatory path for a maintenance crew servicing a CFM LEAP-1B engine on a Boeing 737 MAX begins with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issuing airworthiness directives (ADs). The FAA’s 2020-05-11 AD (Initial return-to-service requirements) and the 2024-01-02 AD (continued airworthiness for the engine mount) set the baseline compliance obligations for operators and maintenance personnel【142e141d-9abb-4019-a280-8d6be8a1e409】【fe83242a-e2a4-4f64-8fdb-eb5e18419f9c】. The FAA’s 2022-03-07 AD requires inspection of the AOA sensor bracket, which includes the forward pylon structure that supports the LEAP-1B engine【fe83242a-e2a4-4f64-8fdb-eb5e18419f9c】. 

CFM International, as the engine manufacturer, issues its own ADs that supplement FAA requirements. CFM’s 2023-14 AD mandates a fan-blade inspection on the LEAP-1B engine, which operators must perform in conjunction with FAA AD compliance【142e141d-9abb-4019-a280-8d6be8a1e409】. 

Once the FAA and CFM ADs are published, the airline’s maintenance organization translates these directives into specific maintenance tasks. The maintenance crew follows the FAA ADs and the CFM ADs, using the Boeing 737-8/9 engine-mount inspection procedures outlined in Chapter 71-21-05 of the 737 MAX maintenance manual【bb84fd20-ee3f-4166-a7b1-b03074c6f3ab】. The crew performs the required inspections, repairs, or replacements, documents the work, and files the necessary reports to satisfy both FAA and CFM regulatory obligations.
